title: Lead Handoff Audit: 12 Checks Before Your Next MQL Goes Cold
subtitle: A 12-minute diagnostic for RevOps and ops leads at 20-80 person agencies. Score the handoff from marketing to sales to delivery, find the stage where MQLs go cold, and walk away with the first fix to run this quarter.

benchmarks.metric: B2B leads never followed up by sales
Increase in lead qualification odds when contacted within 5 minutes vs 30 minutes
benchmarks.source: Harvard Business Review / Lead Response Management Study

benchmarks.metric: Marketing-generated leads sales reps actively work

methodology_anchor.name: Agent-Ready Ops
preconditions: Structured input data. Lead records arrive with the fields sales actually needs to decide, not free-text blobs from a contact form.
Documentable decision logic. Your MQL definition and routing rules are written down somewhere a new hire could read, not living in one rep's head.
Narrow initial scope. The first automation handles a single handoff (form to CRM, CRM to rep, rep to delivery), not the whole funnel at once.
Human-in-the-loop by design. A person reviews edge cases (high-value leads, weird sources, mismatched ICP) before the system makes them disappear into a stale-lead nurture.
methodology_anchor.intro: This assessment scores your lead handoff against the four preconditions for Agent-Ready Ops. Hit all four and you can wire AI into routing, scoring, and follow-up without losing leads. Miss one and any automation you build on top will leak in the same places your current process does.

proof_card.sample_top_leak: lead routing (~9 hrs/week of MQLs sitting unassigned > 24h)

answers.label: Under 20 people, founder still touches most leads
20-40 people, dedicated AM/sales but no RevOps owner
40-80 people, RevOps function exists but is stretched
80+ people, full RevOps team and defined process owners

questions.text: How consistently does your inbound form capture the fields sales actually needs to decide if a lead is real?

answers.label: 1. Name and email only, everything else is a back-and-forth
2. Some firmographics but free-text fields dominate
3. Most fields are there, sales fills the gaps on the first call
4. Decision-ready fields are required, optional fields are clearly marked
5. Form is structured, validated, and sales can route without asking the lead anything

questions.text: How reliably do you know where a lead came from by the time it hits the CRM?

answers.label: 1. We guess based on the rep's memory
2. Source is captured but inconsistent across channels
3. Source is captured for paid, missing for organic and referral
4. Source, medium, and campaign are tagged for most leads
5. Full UTM and source attribution on every lead, queryable from day one

questions.text: How automated is the filter that keeps spam, students, and out-of-ICP leads out of the sales queue?

answers.label: 1. Everything goes to sales, they triage manually
2. Basic spam filter, ICP filtering is rep judgment
3. Rules-based filter catches obvious junk, edge cases reach sales
4. Enrichment plus rules filter most non-ICP before routing
5. Filtered, enriched, and scored before a rep ever sees the record

low.headline: Your form is the leak before sales even gets a chance
low.text: If reps have to email back asking for company size or budget, the lead has already cooled by hours or days. Free-text fields and missing firmographics push the qualification work onto people instead of the form. The fix is upstream, not at the rep level.
steps: Audit your top 3 inbound forms and list every field a rep needs to decide if a lead is real
Make those fields required and validated (no 'asdf' in the company field)
Add a hidden source/UTM capture so attribution lands in the CRM without anyone typing it

mid.headline: The form captures most of what matters, junk is the next leak
mid.text: You have the basics covered but spam, students, and out-of-ICP leads are still landing in the sales queue. That tax compounds: every junk lead a rep triages is 3-5 minutes off a real one. A rules layer plus enrichment closes that gap.
steps: Add an enrichment step (Clearbit, Apollo, or similar) at form submit to pull employee count and industry
Write 3-5 hard rules that auto-route obvious non-ICP to a nurture or rejection state
Tag remaining edge cases for human review instead of dumping them on a rep's list

high.headline: Intake is clean, the frontier is signal density
high.text: Keep sharpening. The next gain is using the data you're already capturing to predict which leads close, not just which ones are real.
steps: Layer behavioral data (pages visited, content downloaded, time on site) onto firmographics
Score leads on closed-won patterns from the last 12 months, not gut-feel weights
Feed the score back into routing so your best rep gets the best leads, not the first ones

operator_brief.headline_number: ~6 hrs/week of rep time recoverable from triaging junk and chasing missing form data
operator_brief.lever: Move qualification work from reps into the form and an enrichment step at submit.
talking_points: Every junk lead a rep triages is 3-5 minutes that should have gone to a real one
Free-text fields are the single biggest reason MQLs sit unworked past 24 hours
Enrichment at submit costs less per lead than the rep time it saves
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: One-week test: add 3 required structured fields to your top inbound form and measure rep time-to-first-touch before and after.

questions.text: How fast does a new MQL get a first human touch during business hours?

answers.label: 1. Often more than 24 hours, no SLA tracked
2. Same day on most leads, no real measurement
3. Within 4 hours on most leads, SLA is informal
4. Within 1 hour on most leads, SLA is tracked weekly
5. Under 5 minutes on inbound, automated alerting and SLA reporting

questions.text: How documented is the logic that decides which rep gets which lead?

answers.label: 1. Whoever sees it first grabs it
2. Round-robin in someone's head, no written rules
3. Rules exist but live in Slack or one person's brain
4. Written routing rules by territory, vertical, or deal size
5. Rules are in the CRM, version-controlled, and auditable

questions.text: How does your system handle leads that come in after hours or on weekends?

answers.label: 1. They wait until Monday morning
2. Someone on rotation checks email occasionally
3. Auto-reply confirms receipt, no qualification until next day
4. Auto-reply plus an AI or chatbot pre-qualifies and books time
5. After-hours leads are scored, routed, and have meetings booked before Monday

low.headline: Speed-to-lead is where you're hemorrhaging the most
low.text: The HBR data on this is brutal: contact in 5 minutes vs 30 minutes is a 21x difference in qualification odds. If you're measuring in hours or days, you've already lost most of the leads you paid to generate. This is the highest-ROI fix on the list.
steps: Set an SLA (60 minutes is a reasonable floor) and put a dashboard on it
Auto-route by simplest possible rule (round-robin by region or vertical) and revisit later
Add an instant auto-reply that confirms receipt and offers a calendar link

mid.headline: Routing works but SLA enforcement and after-hours are weak
mid.text: You're getting to leads in hours, not days, but inbound that hits at 6pm Friday is still dead by Monday. The gap between 'mostly fast' and 'consistently under 5 minutes' is where you stop losing deals to whoever responded first.
steps: Add automated alerting when a lead sits unworked past SLA
Wire an after-hours AI or chatbot to qualify and book time on inbound
Audit your last 30 days of inbound and tag every lead that breached SLA, by rep

high.headline: You're winning on speed, the frontier is intent-based routing
high.text: Keep sharpening. Once speed is solved, the next gain is matching the right rep to the right lead based on intent signals, not load balancing.
steps: Score leads on intent signals (pricing page visits, demo requests, content depth) and route hot leads to senior reps
Build a fast-lane queue that bypasses normal routing for high-intent inbound
Track win rate by rep-to-lead-segment match and rebalance routing quarterly

operator_brief.headline_number: ~9 hrs/week of MQLs sitting unassigned past 24 hours
operator_brief.lever: Set a sub-60-minute SLA, automate the alerting that enforces it, and put after-hours leads on a qualification path.
talking_points: Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes is a 21x lift in qualification odds versus 30 minutes (HBR data)
Every lead that sits past SLA is a lead a competitor with faster routing has already touched
After-hours leads are 30-40% of weekly inbound for most agencies and most of them go cold
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Two-week test: add an SLA dashboard and an after-hours auto-reply with a calendar link, measure meetings booked from off-hours leads before and after.

questions.text: How clearly is your MQL definition written down and shared between marketing and sales?

answers.label: 1. No written definition, marketing and sales argue about it
2. A doc exists but nobody references it
3. Definition is shared but applied inconsistently
4. Definition is written, referenced in routing rules, and reviewed quarterly
5. Definition is encoded in the CRM and audited against closed-won data

questions.text: When sales disqualifies a lead, how does that signal get back to marketing?

answers.label: 1. It doesn't, leads just disappear
2. Ad-hoc Slack messages between AM and marketer
3. Disqualification reason is captured in CRM but rarely reviewed
4. Reasons are captured, reviewed monthly, and feed campaign decisions
5. Closed-loop reporting drives spend reallocation in real time

questions.text: How does your lead scoring model handle a new lead?

answers.label: 1. No scoring, reps eyeball every record
2. Basic scoring based on form fields only
3. Scoring uses firmographics and a few behavior signals
4. Scoring is built from closed-won patterns and updated quarterly
5. Scoring uses fit + intent + engagement, with a feedback loop to retrain weights

low.headline: Marketing and sales aren't qualifying the same lead
low.text: If your MQL definition isn't written down, marketing is celebrating volume and sales is complaining about quality, and both are right. This is the cheapest fix on the list: a 60-minute meeting and a shared doc.
steps: Pull the last 20 closed-won deals and write down the 5-7 fields they share
Codify that as your MQL definition and have both marketing and sales leads sign off
Add a disqualification reason field to your CRM and require it on every closed-lost

mid.headline: Definition exists, the feedback loop is broken
mid.text: You've defined MQL but disqualifications aren't making it back to the source. Marketing keeps producing the same low-fit leads because nothing is telling them to stop. This loop is what turns scoring from theory into a real lever.
steps: Make disqualification reason required, with 5-7 standardized options
Run a monthly review of disqualification reasons by source
Cut or reallocate spend on the top 2 sources producing the most unqualified leads

high.headline: Qualification is sharp, sharpen the model next
high.text: Keep sharpening. The next gain is moving from rules-based scoring to a model that learns from your actual win patterns.
steps: Pull 12 months of closed-won and closed-lost data and rebuild scoring weights from it
Add intent data (third-party intent, on-site behavior) to the fit-based model
Set a quarterly cadence to audit scoring accuracy against actual outcomes

operator_brief.headline_number: ~15-25% of marketing spend going to sources that produce structurally low-fit leads
operator_brief.lever: Close the loop between sales disqualification reasons and marketing source-level spend.
talking_points: Without a written MQL definition, marketing optimizes for volume and sales optimizes for quality, and they pull in opposite directions
Disqualification reasons are the cheapest data source you have and most agencies don't capture them
A scoring model built from your own closed-won data beats any vendor's generic scoring template
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: One-month test: require disqualification reason on every closed-lost, then run a source-level review and reallocate the bottom-source budget.

questions.text: How clearly is your CRM the single source of truth for lead status?

answers.label: 1. Reps track leads in personal spreadsheets and the CRM is a graveyard
2. CRM has most data but parallel trackers exist
3. CRM is primary, exports happen for reporting
4. CRM is the source of truth, dashboards pull live from it
5. CRM is fully integrated with marketing, billing, and delivery tools

questions.text: How does your system handle duplicate lead records?

answers.label: 1. Duplicates are everywhere, reps work around them
2. Someone cleans them manually every few weeks
3. Dedupe rules exist but miss edge cases (different emails, same company)
4. Automated dedupe on submit, with edge cases flagged for review
5. Fuzzy matching across email, domain, and phone, with audit trail

questions.text: By the time a lead reaches sales, how clean is the record?

answers.label: 1. Reps spend the first 10 minutes fixing the record before they can work it
2. Records are usable but need cleanup before reporting
3. Most fields are right, edge cases need rep judgment
4. Records are validated and enriched before they hit the rep's queue
5. Records are decision-ready, no cleanup or enrichment needed by the rep

low.headline: Your CRM isn't running the handoff, people are
low.text: If reps are working out of spreadsheets and the CRM is where leads go to die, no automation you build on top will hold. The CRM has to be the source of truth before scoring, routing, or AI can do anything useful.
steps: Audit the gap between your CRM and the spreadsheets reps actually use, list every field that's missing
Pick one process (lead intake) and make CRM the only acceptable system for that workflow
Set a 30-day deadline to retire parallel trackers, with leadership backing

mid.headline: CRM works, dedupe and data quality are the gaps
mid.text: Duplicates and dirty records cost reps time on every touch. The fix is mostly automation at the intake layer, not training reps to be more careful.
steps: Implement automated dedupe on submit with fuzzy matching across email and domain
Add validation rules that reject obviously bad data at the form level
Run a monthly data-quality report and assign cleanup to a named owner

high.headline: Systems are tight, the frontier is integration depth
high.text: Keep sharpening. The next gain is connecting the CRM to delivery and billing so the full lifecycle is visible without exports.
steps: Wire CRM to your delivery PM tool so closed-won deals create project records automatically
Push billing and invoicing data back into the CRM for full LTV visibility
Build a single dashboard that shows lead-to-cash time by source

operator_brief.headline_number: ~4-7 hrs/week of rep time spent cleaning up records before they can work them
operator_brief.lever: Move data validation, enrichment, and dedupe upstream of the rep, into the intake and routing layer.
talking_points: Every minute a rep spends cleaning a record is a minute not spent on a real conversation
Duplicate records distort reporting, scoring, and territory assignment in ways nobody traces back to the root cause
CRM as source of truth is a precondition for any AI or automation layer, not a nice-to-have
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Two-week test: add automated dedupe and field validation at intake, measure rep time-to-first-touch before and after.

questions.text: How automated is the handoff from sales to delivery when a deal closes?

answers.label: 1. Sales emails delivery and hopes someone reads it
2. A manual checklist gets filled out, kickoff happens days later
3. Templated handoff doc but creation is manual
4. Closed-won triggers automated record creation in delivery tools
5. Full automation: project space, folders, assignments, and kickoff scheduled in minutes

questions.text: How much context from the sales process actually makes it to the delivery team?

answers.label: 1. Almost none, the client has to repeat themselves on kickoff
2. Basic deal info, but objectives and goals get lost
3. Notes are passed but in different formats every time
4. Structured handoff doc captures goals, objections, and risk flags
5. Full transcript or summary plus structured context lands automatically

questions.text: Score your team on what the client experiences in week one after signing.

answers.label: 1. Silence for days, then a confused intro call
2. Welcome email goes out but real work starts later
3. Kickoff happens within 5-7 days, mostly on track
4. Welcome, access, and kickoff land in the first 48 hours
5. Polished onboarding sequence, kickoff inside 24 hours, no client surprises

low.headline: The handoff to delivery is where you lose the trust you just built
low.text: Sales closes the deal, delivery ghosts the client for three days, and the relationship starts with friction. This is the most fixable category because the trigger (closed-won) is already in your CRM, you just need to wire what happens next.
steps: Build a closed-won trigger that creates the project record, folder structure, and kickoff invite automatically
Define what context delivery actually needs (goals, decision-makers, risk flags) and add those as required fields in sales
Send a templated welcome email within 1 hour of close, signed by the delivery lead

mid.headline: Handoff works, context loss is the leak
mid.text: Records get created and kickoff happens, but the delivery team is still asking the client to repeat themselves on the first call. The fix is making sales context structured, not adding more meetings.
steps: Standardize the handoff doc with 6-8 required fields covering goals, risks, and decision history
Push call transcripts or summaries into the project record automatically
Run a quarterly review of kickoff calls and flag when delivery asked something sales already knew

high.headline: Handoff is dialed, the frontier is proactive onboarding
high.text: Keep sharpening. The next gain is using the data you've already captured to anticipate client questions in week one, not just answer them.
steps: Build a first-30-days client comms sequence triggered by closed-won, customized by deal size and vertical
Surface risk flags from sales notes proactively in the delivery dashboard
Track time-from-signed-to-first-deliverable as a metric and shrink it quarter over quarter

operator_brief.headline_number: ~45 minutes of admin per closed deal collapsible to under 2 minutes with automated handoff
operator_brief.lever: Wire closed-won as the trigger for project creation, folder setup, and kickoff scheduling.
talking_points: The handoff is the most expensive moment of the relationship because trust is highest and friction is most visible
Every piece of context sales captured and delivery has to ask for again is a client-perceived failure
Automating the handoff isn't about saving 45 minutes, it's about protecting the first-week client experience
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Two-week test: build a single closed-won automation (project record + folder structure + welcome email) and measure time-to-kickoff before and after.
